title: Electrical Probing of Sub-Néel Spin Dynamics in Two-Dimensional Antiferromagnets Using Graphene Heterostructures
authors: Adrián García-Martín, Sara Gullace, Nicolás Montenegro-Pohlhammer, María José Martínez-Pérez, Rocío Sánchez-de-Armas, Carmen J. Calzado, Enrique Burzurí
abstract: Low-dimensional antiferromagnetic van der Waals materials have emerged as a versatile platform for exploring exotic spin dynamics and magnetic phases, yet electrically accessing these phenomena remains a major challenge because of their vanishing net magnetization and highly insulating nature. Here, we demonstrate that graphene can act as an ultrasensitive electrical transducer of hidden spin dynamics in two-dimensional antiferromagnets. By integrating graphene with the van der Waals antiferromagnet FePS$_3$, low-temperature transport measurements combined with magnetic-field and gate-voltage control reveal multiple resistance anomalies well below the Néel temperature. Their distinct temperature, magnetic-field, and carrier-density dependences enable us to associate these anomalies with magnon excitations and with a low-temperature magnetic reconfiguration of the antiferromagnetic state, both of which remain largely inaccessible to conventional magnetometry. Density functional theory calculations further show that competing antiferromagnetic spin configurations in FePS$_3$ are nearly degenerate in energy while producing markedly different electronic responses in the adjacent graphene layer. The pronounced electrostatic tunability of these signatures demonstrates that graphene directly transduces interfacial magnetic dynamics into an electrical signal. Our work establishes graphene/antiferromagnetic van der Waals heterostructures as a versatile platform for the electrical readout of spin dynamics in two-dimensional magnets.
summary: This work pioneers the use of graphene as an electrical transducer to probe hidden spin dynamics in 2D antiferromagnets like $	ext{FePS}_3$. By measuring transport resistance under magnetic and gate-voltage control, the authors identify signatures corresponding to magnon excitations and magnetic phase changes. This establishes a versatile platform for electrical readout of magnetism in 2D quantum materials.
main_problem: The primary challenge addressed is the electrical probing of subtle, hidden spin dynamics within low-dimensional, insulating antiferromagnetic (AFM) van der Waals materials.
main_result: The authors demonstrate that graphene acts as an ultrasensitive electrical transducer, allowing the measurement of magnon excitations and magnetic reconfigurations in the AFM state via transport anomalies.
method: The study combines low-temperature transport measurements (measuring resistance $R$ vs. $T, H, V_g$) with first-principles Density Functional Theory (DFT) calculations.
model_or_system: The physical system is a graphene/antiferromagnetic van der Waals heterostructure, specifically using $	ext{FePS}_3$. DFT models the electronic structure and magnetic configurations (zigzag1/zigzag2) of the interface, while transport calculations use the Boltzmann theory.
key_observables: Resistance anomalies ($R$ dips), temperature dependence of anomalies, magnetic field dependence of the Néel temperature ($T_N$), and gate-voltage tunability of electrical signatures.
important_parameters: Low temperatures (down to 3 K), magnetic fields (up to 14 T), and electrostatic gate voltages ($V_g$).
main_assumptions: The current flow is assumed to be predominantly through the graphene layer, and DFT calculations rely on the rigid band approximation for conductivity modeling.
figures_summary: Figures show transport measurements ($R$ vs. $T, H, V_g$) revealing multiple resistance anomalies below $T_N$, and DFT calculations illustrate the magnetic configurations and electronic response of the interface.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical challenge, presents the experimental setup (GFET measurements), details the observed magnetic transitions (Néel, phase reorientation), and supports these findings with detailed DFT calculations of the electronic coupling.
why_interesting: The ability to transduce subtle, non-magnetic spin dynamics into a measurable electrical signal is highly relevant for developing novel quantum sensors and reading out quantum states in magnetic materials.
